CHIEF COMPLAINT
Big toe pain and redness

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports big toe pain and redness that has been occurring off and on for approximately two weeks, with significant worsening over the past week. Patient attended a trade show convention during this time and was unable to walk the halls due to severe pain. Pain is described as throbbing in nature with occasional sharp stabbing quality, particularly with movement. Patient reports walking on heel to avoid bending the toe. Pain is exacerbated by light pressure, including sheets at night and during rolling over in bed. Denies specific traumatic injury. Became concerned when toe became red and warm to touch. Has tried ibuprofen 2 tablets daily without relief.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Endorses pain with light pressure and movement of big toe. Denies stomach problems. Otherwise not documented.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Denies stomach problems

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen 2 tablets daily

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient is employed in a job requiring standing on feet daily. Actively rides bikes on trails, pedaling with back of feet. Usually wears flip-flops. Enjoys fishing and Mexican food.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Inspection: Big toe erythematous, warm to touch. Palpation reveals bone spur on dorsal aspect of big toe joint. Range of motion testing: dorsiflexion produces pain; plantarflexion produces pain, worsening at 20 degrees. Anterior-posterior motion elicits pain with palpable grinding sensation. Palpation between first and second toes produces mild pain. Palpation on lateral aspect of big toe produces significant pain.

RESULTS
X-ray of foot: Large dorsal spur on big toe joint with significant cartilage loss.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus with arthritis. Prescribed meloxicam once daily for anti-inflammatory effect. Patient counseled on potential gastric irritation and instructed to discontinue medication and call if heartburn or epigastric pain develops. Shoe orthotic insert prescribed. Patient instructed to continue regular work and daily activities. Follow-up appointment in two weeks to assess response to conservative treatment. Discussed potential escalation to more invasive treatments including intra-articular injection, joint debridement surgery, or joint fusion if conservative management unsuccessful.
